records.name_note: Admissible sources split on both the spelling and the exact common name for Sorghastrum nutans. NC State's Common Name(s) field is a two-entry stacked list ("Indiangrass" / "Yellow Indiangrass") whose order matches the page-title parenthetical "(Indiangrass, Yellow Indiangrass)," and NC State's own body prose also leads with the one-word spelling "Indiangrass" -- so on NC State's page that is a genuine lead. However, three of the other admissible domains' dedicated single-species pages instead lead with the two-word spelling: Clemson HGIC titles its page "Indian Grass (Sorghastrum nutans)," Missouri Botanical Garden's affirmative "Common Name:" field reads "Indian grass" (with its Common Names tooltip listing only "Indian grass" and "wood grass," no Yellow Indiangrass variant), and RHS's plant-profile subtitle also reads "Indian grass" (with "wood grass" listed under Other common names). Because a majority of the admissible domains' dedicated single-species pages (three of five) lead with "Indian grass," that name was chosen as common_name over NC State's "Indiangrass." Separately, University of Maryland Extension runs its own dedicated single-species page titled "Yellow Indiangrass," matching NC State's second stacked entry -- so "Yellow Indiangrass" is a real, source-backed alternate common name for this species (NC State's second stacked entry and UMD's page title), just not the one chosen as primary here.

records.name_note: Sources split on lead name. NC State's Common Name(s) field lists five alphabetized, stacked entries (Beargrass, Bear's Grass, Button Eryngo, Button snake-root, Rattlesnake Master), repeated in the same order in its page-title parenthetical; with three or more alphabetized entries no entry is a marked primary, and NC State's own body prose introduces the species as 'Beargrass, or rattlesnake master,' naming both without clearly favoring either. Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder marks a single primary in an affirmative 'Common Name:' field reading 'rattlesnake master' (with a longer four-name list behind its tooltip: rattlesnake master, button snakeroot, rattlesnake-master, rattlesnake's master), and its own body prose also leads with 'rattlesnake-master.' RHS likewise marks a single primary, giving 'rattlesnake-master' as the plant-profile subtitle and page title, with button eryngo, button snakeroot, and rattlesnake's master listed separately under 'Other common names.' Because the two sources that mark a primary common name (MoBot and RHS) both lead with rattlesnake master, that name is used as common_name; 'Beargrass' is recorded here as NC State's alphabetically-first alternate rather than promoted. All three sources are dedicated single-species pages -- what separates them is whether they mark a primary, not page scope.
unknowns: No admissible source (NC State, MoBot, RHS) mentions toxicity, poisonous parts, or pet/animal safety for Eryngium yuccifolium at all -- NC State's Plant Type list carries no 'Poisonous' tag and its Problems tags carry no 'Poisonous to Humans' tag, so there is no Poison block to capture. toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null rather than inferred.

No admissible source gives day/night temperature ranges or a chill-damage onset temperature; only NC State's USDA Plant Hardiness Zone rating (3a-8b) is available, which is a hardiness/survival rating, not a damage-onset figure, so day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, and chill_damage_f are left null per the rule against deriving these from zone ratings.

No admissible source states a numeric fc light level, species-specific direct-sun-hour figure, or humidity percentage/need for this species; only the generic 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' NC State light-category legend text exists, which the schema instructions say not to use for direct_sun_hours_max. light_fc_min, light_fc_good, direct_sun_hours_max, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, and humidity_pct_max are left null.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are left null: NC State's Soil pH field lists open-ended Acid (<6.0) and Alkaline (>8.0) bands alongside Neutral (6.0-8.0), and RHS's pH field independently lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' as acceptable -- both sources indicate tolerance across the full range in both directions, so no ceiling or floor is set.

water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis are all left null. This is an in-ground garden-bed perennial, not a plant given container/day-interval watering guidance by any admissible source. The only structured watering field found is MoBot's 'Water: Dry to medium', which is mid-scale per the schema rule and does not itself support any of the four enum values, so it is not used to populate water_regime.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength are left null -- no admissible source gives a fertilizing schedule, interval, or dilution strength for this species; MoBot's Culture text only warns that overly fertile soil causes the plant to sprawl.

Transplant note (taproot species, per task instructions): MoBot's Culture section states 'This is a taprooted plant which transplants poorly and is best left undisturbed once established' -- captured as supporting context for soil_base/soil_drainage but there is no dedicated schema field for transplant behavior, so it is recorded here rather than fabricating a field.

soil_drainage is set to moderate based on NC State's Soil Drainage field pairing 'Good Drainage' with 'Moist' (plus 'Occasionally Dry'), per the schema's explicit mapping of that NC State combination to moderate. This sits in some tension with MoBot's Culture text ('Easily grown in average, dry to medium, well-drained soils... Prefers dryish, sandy soils') and Water field ('Dry to medium'), and RHS's bare 'Well-drained' Moisture field with a cultivation note to grow in 'dry, well-drained, poor to moderately fertile soil' and 'Protect from winter wet' -- all of which lean toward a drier/faster-draining reading. Disclosed here since the sources are not in full agreement on how wet-tolerant this species is.

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name for this exact species. NC State's Common Name(s) field is a 7-entry alphabetized list (False Indigo, Thin-Pod White Wild Indigo, White False Indigo, White Indigo, White Wild Indigo, Wild Indigo, Wild White Indigo) with no primary marked -- its first entry, 'False Indigo', is an alphabetization artifact and a genus-umbrella name (NC State's page for the catalog's sibling Baptisia australis, Blue False Indigo, carries 'False Indigo' in its own title list); NC State's own body prose leads with 'Wild white indigo.' RHS's dedicated single-species page is titled 'Baptisia alba | white false indigo', with white false indigo as its plant-profile lead. Clemson's Baptisia factsheet heads its species subsection with the scientific name and its prose says 'This species is known as white false indigo or wild white indigo.' MoBot's displayed 'Common Name:' field shows the umbrella 'false indigo', but its Common Names popup lists false indigo, white false indigo, thin-pod white wild indigo, and its Noteworthy Characteristics prose reads 'Baptisia alba commonly called white false indigo'. UGA's Native Plants for Georgia wildflowers publication -- a multi-species page -- heads its Baptisia alba section 'White Wild Indigo', and that name is also NC State's fifth list entry. common_name is White False Indigo: it is the lead of the one dedicated single-species page that marks a primary (RHS) and the name Clemson's and MoBot's prose lead with; White Wild Indigo (UGA's section heading, NC State's list) and Wild White Indigo (NC State's prose) are sourced alternates. It does not collide with Blue False Indigo (b37).
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page carries a "Poisonous to Humans:" block (its Plant Type list also includes "Poisonous," and the page-top badge reads "This plant has low severity poison characteristics"). This block is HUMAN-scoped, not cat/dog-scoped: Poison Severity is Low; Poison Symptoms (verbatim): "THIS PLANT CAUSES ONLY LOW TOXICITY IF EATEN. Poisonous through ingestion. All parts are poisonous. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea."; Poison Toxic Principle: "Baptisin and cytisine"; Causes Contact Dermatitis: "No"; and the full Poison Part list (not truncated): Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. NC State's Plant Type field lists Herbaceous Perennial, Native Plant, Perennial, Poisonous, Wildflower. No admissible source (NC State, Clemson, MoBot, UGA, RHS) carries a Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag, or any other cat/dog-scoped toxicity statement, for this species — NC State's only Problem-For tag is "Poisonous to Humans." A UGA search snippet (outside the admissible fetch) referenced toxicity to "livestock and humans," which likewise does not name cats or dogs.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: the only admissible-source toxicity evidence found (NC State's Poisonous to Humans block) is human-scoped; no source names cats or dogs specifically, so per the cat/dog-scoping rule this stays null rather than being inferred from the human toxicity data.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's only hour figures ('6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day', '2-6 hours') come from its site-wide Light-category legend field, which the rules exclude as a source for this field; no species-specific prose gives an hour count.

soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State's Soil pH field is the open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' band, which sets no floor or ceiling per the rules. RHS gives only the categorical 'Acid or Neutral' with no numeric bounds, so there is no closed numeric band from any admissible source to check against.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good/humidity_need/humidity_pct/day-night temperature fields/water_dry_down_target/water_check_depth_cm/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_estimate_basis/chill_damage_f/cool_rest_note/fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_active_months/fertilize_strength all left null: no admissible source frames this in-ground native perennial's care in foot-candles, percent humidity, daily temperature ranges, dry-down depth/day-interval terms, an onset chill-damage temperature, or any fertilizing schedule/strength.

NC State also auto-generates one alias page per listed common name (e.g. /plants/baptisia-alba/common-name/white-wild-indigo/, /plants/baptisia-alba/common-name/white-false-indigo/) for this species; these alias pages were not treated as independent sources of primacy, per the rule that such pages carry no primacy signal.

No admissible source filed this species under var. macrophylla; that variety appears only as its own separate taxon (e.g. RHS's Baptisia alba var. macrophylla page and MoBot's separate taxonid 280691 entry), which was not used for this Baptisia alba (species-level) record.

2026-09-03 landing: common_name changed from 'White Wild Indigo' to 'White False Indigo'. The auditor kept the value but its only citation was a synthesized UGA heading inside a multi-species publication, and the auditor's own findings show RHS's dedicated page title, Clemson's prose and MoBot's prose all leading with white false indigo -- the same lead-name rule that decided b56's names. The fabricated Clemson 'Also Known As' quote (caught by the mechanical check) is replaced by the page's real sentence, the truncated Baptisia australis title is completed, the UGA heading is quoted as it renders, and scientific_name_accepted's bare 'Correct' quote is replaced by RHS's title line.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the lead common name, but all three dedicated single-species pages converge on a "Rough(-...)" variant, not "Wrinkleleaf Goldenrod." NC State's Common Name(s) list carries seven alphabetized entries with none marked primary, so its first entry is an ordering artifact -- but NC State's own body prose calls the plant "Rough-Leaf Goldenrod." Missouri Botanical Garden's affirmative "Common Name:" field designates "rough goldenrod," and its Noteworthy Characteristics text also lists "rough goldenrod, rough-stemmed goldenrod or wrinkle-leaved goldenrod," in that order. RHS's dedicated species profile (not the 'Fireworks' cultivar page) gives "rough-stemmed goldenrod" as its plant-profile subtitle. "Wrinkleleaf Goldenrod" appears only as one of NC State's seven unranked list entries and carries no primacy from any source, so it was not used as common_name. Bare "Goldenrod" is excluded as a genus-umbrella entry on NC State's list, not a species-distinguishing name. RHS's page for this species is otherwise sparse and does not render an "Other common names" list.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: none of the ten admissible domains carry a Poison block or any cat/dog toxicity statement for Solidago rugosa; NC State's species page (plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/solidago-rugosa/) has no Poison Severity/Poison Symptoms/Poison Part fields at all, unlike some other NC State entries.

day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min/good, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis, water_dry_down_target, and all fertilize_* fields left null: no admissible source frames this in-ground native perennial's care in houseplant-style temperature, humidity, light-meter, or countdown-watering/fertilizing terms.

water_regime left null: the only structured watering field found, Missouri Botanical Garden's 'Water: Medium to wet,' is a mid/upper structured tag rather than a WATERING-statement sentence, so per the water_regime rule it was not used to set a value. Disclosed here as a counterpoint suggesting the plant leans toward the wetter side of average moisture; MoBot's Culture prose ('medium to wet, well-drained soils') and its Tolerate tag 'Wet Soil' point the same direction without meeting the rule's bar for a watering statement.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's only hour figures ('Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)', 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)') are the site-wide light-category legend text repeated on every NC State plant page, not species-specific prose, so per the rule they were excluded from this field (though the tags themselves were used to support outdoor_sun_exposure).

soil_ph_min left null: NC State lists an open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' soil pH band for this species in addition to the closed 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' band, so no floor was set. RHS's species page (rhs.org.uk/plants/46560/solidago-rugosa/details) carries no Soil pH field at all, so no cross-check against RHS was possible in either direction; the 8.0 ceiling from NC State's Neutral band is therefore unverified against RHS but not contradicted by it either.

chill_damage_f and cool_rest_note left null: no admissible source states a damage-onset temperature or a cool-rest/dormancy temperature range. NC State gives only a USDA hardiness zone range (4a-8b), which is a survival rating, not a damage-onset figure, per the rule.

RHS's dedicated species page (rhs.org.uk/plants/46560/solidago-rugosa) is sparse: it renders only the H1 binomial, the 'rough-stemmed goldenrod' plant-profile subtitle, a Family field ('Asteraceae'), a Genus description, and a Name Status field ('Correct'). No Other common names list, Position/Aspect, Sun exposure, Soil type/pH/moisture, or ultimate height/spread fields render on the page (confirmed both via fetch and via the accessibility tree of the live page), so RHS could not support or contradict any cultivation values for this species.

Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder page displays a single 'Common Name:' field ('rough goldenrod'); whether a longer Common Names list exists behind a tooltip/popup was not inspected in this research pass.

hgic.clemson.edu/glorious-goldenrod/ names 'Solidago rugosa' but its growing-condition and height figures (2.5-3 ft) read as 'Fireworks'-cultivar-specific, matching the exact trap flagged in the task brief, so this Clemson article was excluded from all species-specific claims rather than risk conflating it with the straight species.

extension.psu.edu, extension.umd.edu, edis.ifas.ufl.edu, ask.ifas.ufl.edu, and fieldreport.caes.uga.edu were searched but no dedicated Solidago rugosa species page with usable structured cultivation or toxicity data was found on any of them; only plants.ces.ncsu.edu, plantfinder.mobot.org (missouribotanicalgarden.org redirects there), and rhs.org.uk yielded admissible species-specific content.

normalizations: 2026-09-03: thirty-ninth batch, the first after the loop resumed at cruise throttle -- native prairie species: Indian Grass, Little Bluestem, Rattlesnake Master, Purple Prairie Clover, White False Indigo, and Rough Goldenrod. Clean first run (12/12 agents, 1.29M subagent tokens). land_check.py and covered.py ran clean; verify_quotes.py 83/83 reachable quotes after repair. The mechanical check caught two fabricated quotes on White False Indigo that the auditor also flagged: a synthesized UGA heading 'White Wild Indigo (Baptisia alba)' (the H2 renders 'White Wild Indigo / Baptisia alba Family: Legume / Fabaceae') and a Clemson 'Also Known As:' field that does not exist (the page's sentence is 'This species is known as white false indigo or wild white indigo.'). Five audit findings, every value kept, plus one flagged common name that changed at landing: Baptisia alba came back as 'White Wild Indigo' on the UGA heading alone, but RHS's dedicated page is titled 'Baptisia alba | white false indigo' and Clemson's and MoBot's prose both lead with white false indigo, so under the catalog's lead-name rule it lands as 'White False Indigo' with White Wild Indigo and Wild White Indigo as sourced alternates (no collision with Blue False Indigo, b37). The other findings were description defects: 'regional' asserted of a name no source calls regional (Indian Grass), a three-entry NC State list called alphabetized-with-no-primary when it is neither (Little Bluestem leads NC State's title and list), an invented 'per the site's own convention' phrase, and a 'dedicated single-species page' discriminator applied to two of three sources that are all dedicated pages (Rattlesnake Master). Six NC State dt labels prepended to dd values were stripped. Purple Prairie Clover and Rough Goldenrod landed with zero findings.
